en: Oṃ.
(Then enter Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra, along with Paraśurāma and Śatānanda.

Vasiṣṭha and Viśvāmitra: O son of Jamadagni, you are dearer to Indra than the performance of sacrifices and charitable works because you destroy his enemies; by you, a hero, this earth has become possessed of a king, just as heaven was by the wielder of the thunderbolt.
We stand here before him; what more need be said? This very King Vaivasvata, who is fond of his sons and has reached the end of his life, himself entreats you.
Therefore, O hero, desist from this futile quarrel; let this instead be so:
the heifer is being prepared, and food with clarified butter is being cooked.
O learned one, you have come to the house of a learned man; please accept our hospitality. //2//
Jāmadagnya: Here I inform you all—why should I not forgive? If Rāma were not possessed of preeminent heroism, you would see for yourselves.
Since even as a child, Rāma was renowned for his wondrous deeds, why did the descendant of Bhṛgu, though unable to endure it, remain after having received such insult?
Who could know this out of respect for his elders? Even if one were a knower, he would not speak; for the vow of a hero is prone to sudden anger toward those who stand before him as they are. (3)
Moreover:

When fame is without room for anything else and shines white in every direction, even if some trivial matter of reproach somehow arises, the foul rumor spread by common folk regarding the noble does not cease by any means. (4)
Vasiṣṭha: Oh child, what is the use of this demoness of a weapon for the rest of your life? You are a master of the Vedas, O son of Jamadagni; follow the pure path, for you are a forest-dweller.

Therefore, gather those four meditations on loving-kindness and the rest which clarify the mind. Indeed, let your mental state named "the Radiant" (jyotiṣmatī), which is free from sorrow, become serene; and let it bring the axe to a close [of ignorance]. From that serenity arises the vision of the inner light—known as "Truth-bearing" (ṛtambharā)—which possesses the capacity to comprehend all objects without depending on external means, which is vigorous, and from which the stains of error have been cast away. That should be practiced by a Brahmin, by which one crosses over death and evil.
Moreover, you are attached to something else. Behold this assembly of sages: here is the elder Yudhājit together with the king and his ministers; and here is the elder Lomapāda.
This ancient lord of the Janakas is a proponent of the Veda who performs sacrifices without ceasing; yet you, free from malice, are his supplicants. (5)
Jāmadagnya: So it is; however, until I have uprooted the very foundation of the enemy, I cannot bear to see the three-eyed God, my preceptor, nor Pārvatī, the wife of my preceptor. (6)
Viśvāmitra: If you are devoted to your elders, then consider me as well. Furthermore, from Hiraṇyagarbha there arose the sages Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, and Aṅgiras—these three.
This Vasiṣṭha is the joy of the Bhṛgus, and you, indeed, are his great-grandson through Aṅgiras. (7)
The son of Jamadagni said:
"I shall perform an expiation for having transgressed against you who are worthy of honor;
however, I will never defile the great vow of wielding the sword. (8)
For it is thus:
since even for one who has attained liberation, the protection of honor is dear by nature; see this of mine as well:
you are my kinsmen, and this is my arm, harsh and marked with the calluses of the bowstring. (9)
Viśvāmitra:
(To himself) For they proclaim my greatness at every step, honoring it indeed.
Even these words that pierce my vital organs truly cause me wonder.
Jāmadagnya: Furthermore, O Blessed One, son of Kuśika!

Since the venerable Vasiṣṭha has his mind fixed solely on Brahman, you, as the ancient preceptor in the deeds of heroes, speak; for it was by him that a weapon was taken up after being born into the pure lineage of Bhṛgu—tell me what is appropriate in this matter. (11)
Vasiṣṭha:
(To himself) Granted that he is great in virtues, yet by nature he is demonic.
Because of its excellence and its all-pervading activity, it indeed perceives in every aspect. //12//
Viśvāmitra: Child, this is what I say:
provoked by the anger of an offense committed by a single individual, you brought about the very destruction of the Kṣatriya race before it had even established its lineage.

Although you were restrained by your own elders, Cyavana and others, while uprooting that very Kṣatriya power which had been produced from the seed of Brahmins for twenty-one times, you desisted only because of your wrath.
O son of Jamadagni, I have indeed desisted from this great undertaking of slaughtering the Kshatriyas, which was prompted by the murder of my father. What is there to conceal here?
Has the axe, like a fragment of lightning, ceased its slaughter of the Kshatriyas and not become the cutter of fuel-sticks and sacrificial wood even for one as dear as you?
Even though its fangs in the form of arrows are withdrawn and its bow-staff is laid aside, it still bears a resemblance to a venomous serpent whose fiery poison has been neutralized.

Thus have I restrained him with words concerning his fall from heaven and other such matters; yet, as before, through their anger and their axes, in time the quarters of the sky will be made dense by great royal lineages, like forests thick with trees risen from a conflagration.

"However, for another reason, Rāma is to have his head cut off. Now, having severed the head of this child of the Raghus who has committed such a rash act, when I have departed again for the forest, may the Raghus and the Janakas be at peace for a long time; alas, let there never again be such an excessive transgression! (16)
Śatānanda: Ah! Is there anyone, even among the kings of Videha or my own dear royal patrons, who has the power to cast even a shadow over me? How much less so my son-in-law?
We householders have long remained here in this home, which is supported by the great pillars of virtuous conduct, just as the domestic fire is maintained within its hearth.
If, however, we should suffer humiliation from another in that regard, then shame on our beloved [son-in-law], shame on our Brahminhood, and shame on the lineage of Aṅgiras! (17)
Viśvāmitra said: "Excellent, my child Gautama, excellent! This King Sīradhvaja has fulfilled his purpose by having you as his domestic priest.
His kingdom does not suffer, it does not decline, and it does not decay;
for you are a learned Brahmin who serves as the protector of his realm and his domestic priest. (18)

Jāmadagnya: O Gautama, it was indeed by you and many other Kṣatriya priests that the world was made to blaze with the splendor of Brahman. However, ordinary lights are extinguished before the extraordinary light.

Śatānanda: (With anger) Ah, you ox! You great sinner who has slaughtered an innocent royal lineage! You of vulgar and distorted conduct! You of loathsome deeds! You unprecedented heretic! You mere wielder of arrows! You back-scratcher! How dare you act so insolently even in this direction? Indeed, are you truly a Brāhmaṇa? Oh, what conduct is this for a "great Brāhmaṇa"—the decapitation of one's own mother and the destruction of fetuses!
And for kings engaged in a sacrificial session, killing is equal to the murder of a Brahmin. //19//
Jāmadagnya: Ah, you wretched reciter of benedictions! You, the family priest of the bordering king! And furthermore, you son of Ahalyā! I am your very arrow-tipped shaft.
Śatānanda: Ah, you wicked, foul-mouthed wretch, disgrace to the lineage of Bhṛgu!
These kings and elders are indeed great in their forbearance by virtue of their majesty; they may well forgive, but Śatānanda will certainly not forgive in this manner. (20)
(Thus he sips water from his water-pot.

Vasiṣṭha: Who is there? Who is here? Let him be appeased, let him be appeased! This is the son of Aṅgiras, whose splendor is as fierce as fire fanned by a whirling fan, who is like Tanūnapāt when sprinkled with the offered speckled butter, and whose light of brahmanic luster is formidable as kindling wood.
Śatānanda: (With agitation; taking up the water for the curse) O members of the assembly! Behold, sirs!
Risen up in fury from this assault by another, I shall swiftly strike down your assailant.
Shattered by the winds agitated by the arising [of my power], I shall reduce the vajra-fire to ashes, as if it were a mere tree. //21//
(Offstage: Be gracious, O Blessed One! Now that you have entered our home, let this unassailable splendor of your asceticism be appeased.
This foremost of the twice-born is praiseworthy for his virtues, and he is our own kinsman; when he has come to our house, how can such a thing be fitting?
Even though he is a learned man, since he has deviated from his path, you should employ the tranquility of the Kshatriya way for the sake of victory in this matter. (22)
Vasiṣṭha: (Pouring out the water of the curse) Dear Śatānanda, let it be as the great king Daśaratha, our relative, has said. Furthermore:
whatever auspiciousness we contemplate in our minds, may you, together with Jābāli and the others, perform the fire-rite for peace.
May that venerable Vāmadeva, indeed reciting the victorious hymns, chants, and sections for the sake of victory, choose [us] together with our disciples. //23//
(Embracing him, he leads him out.

Jāmadagnya: Behold the roars of this youth, who is held in check by a mere Kṣatriya! So, what is the use of him? O Brāhmaṇas who subsist on the favors of the lords of Kosala and Videha, and all you Kṣatriyas whose domain extends across the seven mountain ranges and continents, we say this to you: whoever among you here claims the authority of either asceticism or weaponry, let him, unable to endure the arrogance of this unruly youth, take his measure!
Having turned the earth into a garden where the banners of Niḥsīra and Daśaratha have vanished, Paraśurāma, still insatiable, now subdues even their kinsmen.
(Offstage: O Bhārgava, you are indeed being insulted!
The son of Jamadagni: This man indeed shows indignation toward us out of arrogance, and he is even provoked against Janaka.
(Entering, Janaka:

Through the destruction of my enemies, through the maturation of time, through my mastery of the householder’s duties, and furthermore, through the constant realization of the supreme reality of Brahman—that innate, victorious Kṣatriya splendor of mine which had ceased has now re-emerged and urges our bow toward action once again. 25.
Jāmadagnya: O Janaka!
You are indeed devoted to the Brahmins, you are mature and endowed with righteousness; the Ṛṣi who is not the last among the Vedāntins, the disciple of the Sun, instructed you thus.
If, according to this conduct, you have been approached by me with humility, then why do you, out of delusion and unaware of fear, speak such harsh words? (26)
Janaka: An egg is being broken and yet there is humility? Listen, O members of the assembly!
Born in the lineage of Bhṛgu and supposedly established in asceticism—though he is our enemy, we have long practiced only forbearance toward him here.
But when he repeatedly and unrestrainedly brushes us aside like blades of grass, then let the bow be drawn even against this Brahmin; there is no other recourse. (27)
Jāmadagnya:
(With a scornful laugh of rage) What do you say? "The bow"? How marvelous!

Even while laughing, he sees his axe—which is like a loud burst of sparks from a fire agitated by the sight of the Kṣatriyas, and which is whetted on the whetstone of his enemies' heads—as something to be laughed at.
Puffed up with pride, this wretched Kshatriya, inflated falsely by old age and worn out by decrepitude, prattles on at my request regarding Yajnavalkya. (28)
Janaka:
(With agitation) What need is there for much here?
This [beast] has its fierce-tipped fangs encircled by a tongue-like bowstring, and it emits a terrible, deep, gurgling roar.
May my bow be like his vast belly, which mocks the gaping maw of Death as he yawns while greedily intent on devouring morsels of life. //29//
(Thus he strings the bow.

(Offstage: Cease, O King! How can your hand—the hand of an ancient archer, whose fingers are covered in grey hair and which has incessantly bestowed thousands of cows upon Brahmins in sacrifice—touch an arrow against this twice-born man? 30.

Janaka: Friend, Great King Daśaratha, let him indeed insult us; it is nothing at all—whose heart would be disturbed by a twice-born man speaking harshly? But how can this wretched boy be tolerated, as he cries out so piercingly in our ear with words contrary to the welfare of our child? (31)
Jāmadagnya: Ah, you evil-minded wretch, lowest of Kṣatriyas! You insult me by calling me "boy.
Rise, rise! Until—with your liver, lungs, heart, entrails, sinews, joints, bones, and semen all torn asunder; with your neck and throat reduced to a mass of old flesh and teeth;

and with the foam of blood gushing from the severed veins and arteries of your head as it falls—the axe shall cut you limb from limb like a beast, making a terrible heap of your body as it falls. (32)
(Entering within, Daśaratha: O Bhārgava!
This king of ours remains as he is, yet even his own body does not remain [as it once was].
Since those verbal insults were inflicted upon him, we indeed suffer misery in every way. (33)
Jāmadagnya: And what of it?
Daśaratha: And for that reason, it cannot be forgiven.
Jāmadagnya: You too, like another sovereign lord, are assailing me. Take heed: by my very nature, I am Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, and you are a Kṣatriya.
Daśaratha: Therefore, you shall certainly not be overlooked. The methods for subduing the unsubdued rest with the Kṣatriyas; you are unsubdued, and we are indeed your Kṣatriya rulers.
Be pacified at once! What more is there to be tamed? Where now are the Brahmins devoted to tranquility, and where is this weapon maintained by the Kṣatriya? (34)
Jāmadagnya:
(Laughing) After a long time indeed, Jāmadagnya has found a protector, you Kṣatriyas and kings, who act as his instructors!

Daśaratha: Oh! Is there some delusion here? "Whether one is ignorant, or has fallen into error, or harbors doubt regarding knowledge, he who performs an action that contradicts what is seen or unseen—the teacher is his protector.
But when error and doubt have been dispelled, and knowledge is restored, if the king does not punish the man for his contradictory deed, then this ruin of the subjects has arrived. (35)
Viśvāmitra: Your Majesty has spoken rightly.

If knowledge has not yet arisen, or if it is beset by doubt, or if it is erroneous, then attend upon the feet of Vasiṣṭha. There must certainly be some defect in your knowledge; otherwise, how could such improper conduct occur? If it were purity, you would not be committing sin, for kings do not tolerate [such] wrongdoing. (36)
The son of Jamadagni:
"In matters of dharma, the Veda, and the bow, the Lord is indeed my teacher; for how could Kṣatriyas provide instruction to one who has annihilated all the warrior class?
However, my connection with the venerable Vasiṣṭha is to be honored out of respect for his age, but not out of rivalry; nor is there anyone else superior to me in ascetic power or knowledge. (37)

Vasiṣṭha: A defeat resulting from the offspring of Bhṛgu is not pleasing to us; however, because he is to be protected by us, such a victory over one who is dear to us is indeed pleasing. Behold, there is a violation of the ancient custom within our own house! 38.

O ignoble one, you who have transgressed the bounds of propriety! Even toward Vasiṣṭha, the eternal preceptor of the world, you are unrestrained. Like a rogue elephant, you shall be subdued by us only after we have first attacked you. 39.

Jāmadagnya: Thus have I been insulted. That very wrath, which long remained like a barb lodged in the vital organ of my heart—crushed and compressed by the weight of inner fortitude at the word of the elder—now flares up within me as I stand broken by this humiliation, like the submarine fire (aurvānala) of the ocean when its waters are scattered by the winds at the end of an aeon. (40)
By good fortune, this humiliation has been attained; my anger blazes like an axe upon the earth. Kings have been placed under the power of Daśaratha’s army.
Let there now be a terrible slaughter of the Kṣatriyas, like a dissolution at the end of an age, which shall once again cause the festival of the enraged God of Death for even twenty-one times! 41.
Vasiṣṭha: Alas! Oh, how terrible!
Though he is indeed our own kinsman, yet out of pride he attempts this dreadful deed; how indeed might he become unslayable?
For if he were even once looked upon by me with a corrupted mind, that would surely bring ruin to my dear child, the infant of Bhṛgu’s lineage.

Viśvāmitra: O son of Jamadagni, you consider the power of weapons to be superior to the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*). By thus casting contempt upon the assembly of Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, and by this transgression against my daughter, you cause us pain; yet you are to be protected on account of our kinship.
Therefore, while my right hand, agitated by anger toward you, seeks the water for a curse, my other hand, by the force of former impressions, seeks the bow. (43)
Jāmadagnya: But wait, O Kauśika!

Whether you abide as a bearer of Brahmanic luster, or whether you be an archer according to the custom of your own caste—O sir, with my fierce ascetic heat I shall burn you; on the other hand, let my axe do what is appropriate. (44)
(Offstage: Here I am, sirs; Rāma, the pupil of Kauśika, bows and makes this request:
"May I conquer him who is the enemy of Kārtavīryārjuna—mighty in his victory over the descendant of Pulastya—and the vanquisher of the prowess of the Kṣatriyas; salutations unto you! (45)
Daśaratha: Rāmabhadra has arrived! How indeed can this be?
Janaka: Ah, how excellent! Grant me your permission. May the illustrious Rāmabhadra be victorious!
He is the subduer of the arrogant, this hero is the lord of the world; and we, led by Vasiṣṭha, are all your guarantors in this matter. (46)
Daśaratha:
Indeed, this very day Rāmabhadra was born into the virtuous home of you whose fame is celebrated and who have undertaken the vow of protecting [the sacrificial fires]—you who are worthy of sacrifice.
For even as an infant, he possesses a certain power such that the Brahmins, through whom the past, present, and future are encompassed by the light of knowledge, perceive it within him. (47)

Jāmadagnya: Come! I think you will defeat the son of Jamadagni, O prince. (With a smile) You shall not defeat him; for the son of Reṇukā is difficult to subdue and is your own executioner. For now, let this bow—terrible with the roar of its thick string coiled within the groves of the Brahma-stambha, and practicing the act of devouring all things like the Ghasmara-Kālarudra with arrows that have extinguished the fierce flames of the fire by dousing them with the gushing blood from the throats of slaughtered Kṣatriyas—[be ready]. (48)
(Thus they all exit.
//The Third Act//
